primaryText: Which student did every professor recommend?

alternatives.form: Professor Jones, John; professor Williams, William; professor Peters, Peter ...

comment: Threefold ambiguous, each reading shown by its answer: (12) for the wh-phrase over the term, (13) for the term over the wh-phrase, (14) for the third reading, which chapter III calls functional.

primaryText: Which student did no professor recommend?

alternatives.form: Professor Jones, John; professor Williams, William; professor Peters, Peter ...

comment: The functional answer survives a decreasing term where the list answer does not, so the third reading of (11) is no arrangement of scopes. The page prints the starred list as a second (15) and the text calls it (17); the starred answer is the list.

primaryText: What did two of John's friends give him for Christmas?
comment: The less likely reading asks after a present John got twice; the more likely one asks to specify, for two friends of the addressee's choosing, what each gave him, so the interrogative has more than one complete semantic answer.

primaryText: Where do they have all books written by Nooteboom in stock?
comment: Depending on the context, an exhaustive listing of all decent bookshops or the mention of some bookshop.

primaryText: Whom did John kiss at the party last night?
comment: (20) answers by a rigid name for every questioner; (21) completely only for a questioner who knows who the girl from next door is; (22) is partial unless the information singles out one redhead.

primaryText: Where can I buy an Italian newspaper?
context: Asked by an Italian tourist in your home-town.
comment: The addressee mentions some place where the tourist is likely to find one rather than a complete list.

primaryText: Whom did you talk to? Your father.
context: The questioner knows who their father is.
comment: Your father is not semantically rigid but is pragmatically rigid in the information set of anyone who knows who their father is.

primaryText: Who won the Tour de France in 1980? The one who ended second in 1979.
discourseSegments: Who won the Tour de France in 1980?
The one who ended second in 1979.
context: The questioner has the information that Joop Zoetemelk ended second in the Tour de France of 1979.
comment: Zoetemelk did end second in 1979, so the answer is a true complete pragmatic answer; a questioner who believes Eddy Merckx ended second gets the false complete answer that Merckx won (p. 360).

primaryText: Who won the Tour de France in 1980? The one who won in 1979.
discourseSegments: Who won the Tour de France in 1980?
context: The questioner wrongly believes that Joop Zoetemelk was the winner in 1979.
comment: The proposition expressed, that the 1979 winner won again in 1980, is false, yet it carries to this questioner the true information that Zoetemelk won in 1980: a false proposition can be a true complete pragmatic answer.

primaryText: Who served you when you bought these boots? An elderly lady wearing glasses.
discourseSegments: Who served you when you bought these boots?
context: Asked by the salesmanager of a client; the property applies to a single member of her staff.
comment: The term is neither semantically rigid nor semantically definite but is pragmatically definite and rigid in the salesmanager's information set.

primaryText: From which authors did the editors already receive their contribution to the proceedings? I don't know, but at least they received it from Professor A.
discourseSegments: From which authors did the editors already receive their contribution to the proceedings?
I don't know, but at least they received it from Professor A.
context: The questioner knows that Prof. A. is bound to be the last one to send in his contribution.
comment: (42) is the shorter form of the answer. For this questioner the explicitly non-exhaustive answer gives the exhaustive answer that every contribution has arrived, though the term lacks the pragmatic properties itself.

primaryText: From whom did the organizers already receive a letter of acceptance to attend the conference? At least from Prof. A.
discourseSegments: From whom did the organizers already receive a letter of acceptance to attend the conference?
context: Prof. A. is also always the first to accept an invitation to attend a conference.
comment: The same answer (42) is of little help toward a complete answer to (43): the exhaustive answer to (41) came from the interrogative's abstract, not from the term.

primaryText: Which student was recommended by each professor?

alternatives.form: Professor Jones, Bill; professor Williams, Mary; and professor Peters, John.

comment: (2a) answers the reading with the wh-phrase over the term, (3a) the pair-list reading with the term over the wh-phrase, on which (1) is equivalent to (4) Which professor recommended which student?

primaryText: John knows which student was recommended by each professor
comment: Three readings: knowing the answer (2), knowing the pair-list answer, which requires de dicto knowledge of who the professors are, and knowing of each actual professor which student that individual recommended.

primaryText: John wonders which student was recommended by each professor
comment: On its third reading (6) implies (7), for no professor does John know which student he or she recommended; on its second it implies (8), not for all professors does he.

primaryText: Whom does John or Mary love?
context: John loves Suzy; Mary loves Suzy and Bill.
comment: (13a) is the unique true complete answer on the first reading; on the choice reading both (14a) and (15a) are complete and true answers, as for the disjunction (16) Whom does John love? Or, whom does Mary love?

primaryText: Whom do John and Mary love?
context: John loves Suzy; Mary loves Suzy and Bill.

alternatives.form: John, Suzy; and Mary, Suzy and Bill.

comment: (18a) answers the first reading, (19a) the pair-list reading, the conjunction (20) Whom does John love? And, whom does Mary love?

primaryText: What did two of John's friends give him for Christmas?

alternatives.form: Bill, a watch and a ball; Peter, a book and a pen.

comment: (22) answers the reading with the wh-phrase widest; on the choice reading (23a) is one complete answer, and the gifts of any other two friends would be another (p. 454).

primaryText: Which student was recommended by no professor?
comment: A monotone decreasing term cannot take scope over the wh-phrase: the reading would be answered by answering no question (p. 455).

primaryText: What did at most one of John's friends give him for Christmas?
Bill wonders whom John or Mary loves
comment: Assuming wonder implies not knowing, the choice reading implies (27), Bill knows neither whom John loves nor whom Mary loves, and the widest-scope reading (28), he does not know one of them (p. 456).

primaryText: Bill knows whom John or Mary loves
comment: With the extensional know the choice and widest-scope readings coincide, but only because John or Mary is rigid; with two girls they come apart.

primaryText: Where do they sell Italian newspapers in Amsterdam?
comment: Mention-some when asked by an Italian tourist curious about home; mention-all when asked of an informant by someone setting up a distribution network for foreign newspapers.

primaryText: Who has got a light?
Where can I find a pen?
Where is a pen? On my desk.
comment: (2) is a completely satisfactory mention-some answer. The negative (7) is a true partial answer but no satisfactory mention-some answer, and (8), a possible complete answer, is no possible mention-some answer (p. 532).

primaryText: John knows where a pen is
comment: Paraphrased as (10) For all places where a pen is, John knows that there is a pen at that place, and as (11) For some places where a pen is, John knows that there is a pen at that place; the two differ in truth conditions.

primaryText: John wonders where a pen is
comment: Paraphrased as (13), John wants for all places where a pen is to know whether there is a pen there, and as (14), for some place.

primaryText: Who has a pen? John.
comment: Applying the term of (16) to the abstract (17) gives the proposition (18) that John has a pen, a semantic answer on the mention-some reading.

primaryText: John knows who has a pen
comment: On the mention-some reading paraphrasable as (26) Of someone who has a pen, John knows whether he has a pen, and (28) ... that he has a pen (p. 537). If nobody has a pen it is false on that reading even when John knows nobody has one (p. 538).

primaryText: Where do two unicorns live?

alternatives.form: Bel lives in the wood, and Nap lives near the lake
In the wood, and near the lake.

comment: Belnap's example. Mention-some asks for a place where two unicorns live together, mention-all for all such places, mention-two for two places where two different unicorns live. (35) answers the choice reading as a two-constituent interrogative; (36) is a one-constituent answer to the mention-two interpretation, which is therefore not the choice reading, pace Belnap (p. 540).

primaryText: Maria wonders where they sell Italian newspapers
comment: Mention-some interpretations are possible only under verbs with a human subject tied to typical human concerns.

primaryText: Mario asks where they sell Italian newspapers
comment: Mention-some interpretations are possible only under verbs with a human subject tied to typical human concerns.

primaryText: Mary knows where they sell Italian newspapers
comment: Mention-some interpretations are possible only under verbs with a human subject tied to typical human concerns.

primaryText: What the average grade is depends on what grade each student has got
comment: Under verbs with no human subject and no tie to human concerns only mention-all interpretations are possible, a problem for a semantic approach that posits a mention-some reading.

primaryText: Where you can get gas depends on what day it is
comment: Under verbs with no human subject and no tie to human concerns only mention-all interpretations are possible, a problem for a semantic approach that posits a mention-some reading.

primaryText: Does it matter where a pen is?
comment: Under verbs with no human subject and no tie to human concerns only mention-all interpretations are possible, a problem for a semantic approach that posits a mention-some reading.

primaryText: Who will come is partly determined by who is invited
comment: Under verbs with no human subject and no tie to human concerns only mention-all interpretations are possible, a problem for a semantic approach that posits a mention-some reading.

primaryText: Where can I get gas around here? That depends on what time it is.
discourseSegments: Where can I get gas around here?
That depends on what time it is.
comment: The interrogative gets a mention-some interpretation while the indicative reply involves a mention-all interpretation of the same complement.
